## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

That future you also knows why you can't pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they'd be kind about it, or maybe they'd just make you some food. If you can't picture them at all, make the food yourself (a "no" or a pause counts as food here), and skip pretending to feel some way you don't.

You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don't assume they'll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

Somewhere in your history there's probably a time you handled something hard and came out of it respecting yourself a little. Go find it. What did you do, and what was helping you then? ## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

Finish a hard memory with "And so that's the way it happened!" the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

It doesn't turn the memory into fiction, and it doesn't prove you remember every detail right. Nobody gets let off the hook, either: the case stops, but any repair that's owed is still owed. Keep an ear on the narrator. If they start to sneer, stop. Stop too if you feel more ashamed, or kind of unreal, because telling it colder won't help with that. And if the line works, let it stay one line, then ask what the younger you in that story needs from you now.
